title: Burst-pause criterion derivation for drinkometer measurements of ingestive behavior
author: Serra, File, et al.
materials: Drinkometer-derived data were processed as previously described [6]. Briefly, raw data were extracted and pre-processed with MATLAB (version R2020a, Mathworks, Natick, MA) for (1) estimation of the burst-pause criterion (PC)-dependent microstructural parameters, and (2) calculation of the mean value of each macro- and microstructural parameter for each test session. Macro- and microstructural parameters are described in Alceste et al. [1]. Data analysis of pre-processed drinkometer-derived data was performed using R (version 4.0.3) [3] via RStudio (version 1.3.1093) [4]. The overall probability of inter-suck intervals (ISIs) derived with different PCs was analyzed with a Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival analysis. KM survival curves were generated with survminer R package [5].

Based on a significance level of α = 0.05 (5 %), the null hypothesis of no difference in the time-to-event curves of the ISIs derived with the three considered PCs was rejected. Furthermore, the 50 % probability of the three survival curves appeared to divide the derived ISIs with different quotients of the respective PCs (Fig. 3C). With a PC of 1.3 s, a 50 % inter-suck interval probability was associated with ∼59 % of the observed ISIs (at 0.80 s), while, with a PC of 3.14 and 5.13 s, a 50 % inter-suck interval probability was associated with ∼36 % (at 1.12 s) and ∼28 % (at 1.44 s) of the observed ISIs, respectively. Consequently, a selection of intervals larger than the one corresponding to the intersection point for the definition of the PC might cause the erroneous classification of IBIs as ISIs. Indeed, considering a normal sampling distribution of ISIs, the 50 % inter-suck interval probability should be associated to approximately 50 % of the observed ISIs. Instead, this percentage increased parallelly to the increase of difference between the optimal PC and the alternatively selected interval.

steps.title: Initialize MATLAB environment
steps.instruction: Open MATLAB (R2020a) and add the folder containing the drinkometer‑derived data to the MATLAB path.

steps.title: Visualize raw volume data
steps.instruction: Run the script plot_tdms.m to display raw consumed‑volume traces and identify measurements with artefacts.

substeps.instruction: Set the sampling frequency (Fs) to 1000 Hz.
Set the low‑pass filter cutoff frequency (FOI) to 0.5 Hz.
Set plot_filtered_volume = 1 to plot the filtered volume.
Execute the script for each measurement; the script requires the three files .info, .tdms and .tdms_index generated by the drinkometer.
Inspect the generated figures and discard any measurement showing interferences (e.g., Fig. 1A). Keep only clean recordings (e.g., Fig. 1B).

steps.title: Extract and plot inter‑suck intervals
steps.instruction: Create a table of all inter‑suck intervals (ISIs) and visualise their frequency density for each participant.

substeps.instruction: Open the script create_ISI_table.m.
Set Fs = 1000 Hz and FOI = 0.5 Hz.
Set plot_filtered_volume = 1.
Define the artefact speed threshold as 20 ml s⁻¹; intervals exceeding this are deleted and linearly interpolated.
Set the minimal amplitude of a suck to 0.5 ml s⁻¹ (values below are set to zero).
Set the minimal interval between peaks of sucks to 1 s to avoid counting noise as sucks.
Set the minimal suck size to 1 ml; smaller sucks are excluded as noise.
Run the script for each selected measurement (requires .info, .tdms, .tdms_index).
Open the R markdown file ISI_histograms.Rmd.
Edit the directory variables in the script to point to the folders created by create_ISI_table.m.
Run ISI_histograms.Rmd on the .csv output produced by create_ISI_table.m.
Open the resulting figure to examine the logarithmic frequency‑density plot of ISIs for each participant (Fig. 2).

steps.title: Determine burst‑pause criterion via GMM
steps.instruction: Fit a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to the combined ISI and inter‑burst interval (IBI) distributions to locate the optimal burst‑pause criterion (PC).

substeps.instruction: Open the script GM_for_IBI.m.
Apply the same parameter settings used for create_ISI_table.m (Fs = 1000 Hz, FOI = 0.5 Hz, etc.).
Run the script for each measurement (needs .info, .tdms, .tdms_index).
Inspect the generated figures:

– Figure A shows the Akaike information criterion (AIC) for models with 1, 2, … components (single‑component AIC = 5050). The model with the lowest relative AIC indicates the optimal number of components (two in this data set).

– Figure B displays the probability density functions (PDFs) of log‑transformed intervals for ISIs (left curve) and IBIs (right curve). The local minimum between the two PDFs is the optimal PC; in the present population it is 1.34 s (intersection of the two curves).
Record the optimal PC value (1.34 s) for later use.

steps.title: Validate criterion with Kaplan‑Meier analysis
steps.instruction: Compare ISI survival probabilities obtained with the optimal PC and with alternative arbitrary PCs using a Kaplan‑Meier (KM) analysis.

substeps.instruction: Open the R markdown file KM_survival_analysis.Rmd.
Set the directory variables so that the script can locate the .csv output from create_ISI_table.m.
In the section “Selection of PC models” (lines 37‑49), specify the PC to test:
– Optimal PC = 1.34 s (n = 495 ISIs).
– Arbitrary PC 1 = 3.15 s (n = 838 ISIs).
– Arbitrary PC 2 = 5.13 s (n = 1051 ISIs).
– Optionally, set PC = ∞ to include all ISIs (n = 1671).
Run the script.

Open the generated KM figure (Fig. 3C) to view the survival curves for each PC and to perform a log‑rank test (α = 0.05). The optimal PC shows a significantly shorter time‑to‑event (p < 0.0001) compared with the arbitrary PCs.

steps.title: Generate final data tables using PC
steps.instruction: Create the complete set of macro‑structural and micro‑structural tables applying the selected burst‑pause criterion.

substeps.instruction: Open the script create_all_the_tables.m.

Reuse the same parameter settings as in create_ISI_table.m (Fs = 1000 Hz, FOI = 0.5 Hz, artefact threshold = 20 ml s⁻¹, minimal amplitude = 0.5 ml s⁻¹, minimal interval = 1 s, minimal suck size = 1 ml).
Set the PC to the value determined from the GMM/KM analysis (e.g., 1.34 s).
Run the script for each selected measurement (requires .info, .tdms, .tdms_index).
Open the newly generated tables; they contain the mean macro‑structural parameters and both PC‑independent and PC‑dependent micro‑structural parameters for each drinkometer session.

description: The AIC estimated that two density functions would have had the best fit to the data for explaining the recorded intervals (Fig. 3A). This is in accordance with our previously published work [6,7] but also conceptually aligned to experimental results on microstructure of licking behavior in animal models [8,9]. Indeed, it was previously reported that rodents exhibit three kinds of pauses in their licking behavior: inter-lick intervals, inter-burst intervals, and inter-cluster intervals, which are clusters of bursts separated by longer pauses [10]. While inter-lick intervals can be compared to ISIs of human subjects, there is a question whether the cluster/burst distinction is relevant to human sucking or whether it relates to differences in the topography of responses between the two species. For example, in rodents, the topography is licking and in humans it is sucking. When rodents lick, the tongue, although protruded, occasionally misses the drinking spout and this can lead to some of inter-lick intervals being considered inter-burst intervals [11]. Regardless, in the data presented in this protocol and in Alceste et al. [1], we were able to define at least two distributions accounting for ISIs and IBIs, respectively. We analyzed the data accordingly. In a previous study [7], we reported that an optimal PC of 3 s poorly fitted the data (AIC = 13251.8, n = 126 measurements) [7], while, with the current study population (n = 48 measurements), we achieved an AIC of 4855 with the PC of 1.34 s. Considering that AIC scales with the sample size of the dataset and considering that a smaller AIC value is preferable to a larger one [12,13], this represents an advance in the analysis of drinkometer-derived data. Indeed, the inclusion of a single population of RYGB patients for the prediction of the optimal PC led to a model with a slightly better fit to the current data (4855/48 = 101.14) than the one we achieved in our previous work (13251.8/126 = 105.17).
